note: In another version of the incident, Ravina told Mar bar Rav Ashi, at the very place where it happened, that the corner of his garment had torn. Mar bar Rav Ashi answered: do you think I should throw it off? Doesn't the Master say that human dignity is so great that it overrides a prohibition of the Torah?
why: The Gemara is asking how a Sage could keep wearing a garment he was not allowed to carry. In this version he knew and relied on human dignity, and the Gemara explains that this works because the place was a karmelit, where carrying is forbidden only by rabbinic law.

people.name: Ravina

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage whose garment tore while he was walking.

people.name: Rav bar Shabba
people.about: A Sage who explained before Rav Kahana that human dignity overrides only rabbinic prohibitions.

terms.meaning: The principle that a person need not shame himself in public; the Gemara says it overrides rules made by the Sages, not those written in the Torah.
An area that is neither fully public nor private, where carrying on Shabbat is forbidden only by rabbinic law.

flag: The story is the second version of an incident whose first version, and the tear itself, come before the story begins, so it opens mid-scene.

note: Rabbi Beivai reported, in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, that a mule belonging to the household of Rabbi died and the Sages estimated its blood at a quarter-log. Rabbi Yitzhak bar Bisna objected with a testimony that a carcass's blood is pure, and with an incident told by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira: wild donkeys were killed to feed the lions in the king's stadium, pilgrims waded in their blood up to the knees, and the Sages said nothing to them. Rabbi Beivai fell silent. When Rabbi Zerika asked why, he said his life was like the verse 'you shall have no assurance of your life', which Rabbi Hanin read as one who relies on a baker for bread; he relied on a baker. Rav Yosef later explained that Rabbi Yehuda, decisor for the Nasi's house, ruled by his own tradition.
why: The Gemara has been showing that the Sages' measures are exact, down to a hair; the mule's blood adds the quarter-log measure, and the objection asks whether a carcass's blood makes anyone impure at all.

people.name: Rabbi Beivai
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident of the mule and cannot answer the objection to it.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak bar Bisna

people.name: Rabbi Zerika

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira

terms.meaning: A small liquid measure, the minimum amount of blood that can make a person or thing ritually impure.
An animal that died without proper ritual slaughter; its flesh makes people ritually impure.
The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi held this office.
